newsitem.title: USA: Navistar to close foundry, take charge.
newsitem.headline: Navistar to close foundry, take charge.

text.p: Navistar International Corp. will close its Indianapolis Casting Corp. foundry, which employs 650 people, in late 1998 after local union members rejected a company proposal, the truck and school bus manufacturer said Tuesday.
The move followed the ratification of an extension of Navistar's master contract by 63 percent of voting United Auto Workers (UAW) union members, announced by Navistar late Sunday.
But the company left open the possibility that the Indianapolis foundry could remain open if local members of the UAW seek an agreement with the company.
"If they came back and say, 'We'd like to talk one more time,' I'm always willing to work toward (an agreement)," Navistar Chairman John Horne told reporters.

"There's not a locked door," Jack Laskowski, international vice president of the UAW, added on the conference call held jointly by the company and the union. "I don't think that door is closed. I don't know how long, but I'm sure for a short period of time that's possible."
Navistar and UAW officials gave few details about the proposal at the Indianapolis foundry, except to say that workers' basic, take-home wages and benefits would not have changed under the proposal.

While the Indianapolis foundry workers rejected the Navistar proposal, employees at Navistar's Springfield, Ohio, plant ratified an agreement with the company. That pact will allow Navistar to make production changes at Springfield, which could reduce the work force of 5,000 there.
"The leadership at Springfield stood up and recognized where they had to go and carried that message back to their membership," Laskowski said. "The opposite happened at Indianapolis."

Larry Gigerich, senior adviser for economic and work force development to Indianapolis Mayor Stephen Goldsmith, said city officials will encourage local union and company officials to seek an agreement to keep the foundry open.
"We're going to encourage both sides to talk," he added.
He said the foundry has an annual payroll of about $25 million, excluding benefits. The typical worker at the foundry is about 50 years old and a high school graduate with 20 years' experience.

"With wage levels 50 percent higher than the competition's, however, (the Indianapolis foundry) could no longer stay competitive without a new labor agreement, particularly in the face of future competition from foundries in Latin America, where labor costs are significantly lower," Navistar said.
The foundry's 650 employees make grey-iron castings for engines, Navistar said. The company said it plans to take an unspecified charge in the fourth quarter if the foundry is closed.
The UAW represents about 8,000 employees in Indianapolis; Springfield; Fort Wayne, Ind.; Melrose Park, Ill.; and other locations, the company said.

Approval of a contract at Springfield will allow Navistar to proceed with its previously announced plans to focus its assembly plant there exclusively on the production of medium-duty trucks. Navistar's Chatham, Ontario, plant is focusing on heavy-duty trucks.
Navistar also will introduce and build its next-generation truck in Springfield under a promise made to the union.
Navistar and union officials did not give an exact estimate of work force changes at Springfield, saying much depended upon the success of the products it builds there.
Navistar stock rose $1.44 to end at $23.44 on the New York Stock Exchange.
